title: Desk-Worker Mobility
summary: Fit the desk → Bring work closer → Pause → Change position
subtitle: Build comfortable movement into your workday.

blocks.text: Your calendar happily books back-to-back meetings, as if shoulders came with a mute button. A workable movement plan starts by noticing where your day leaves room to change position.
Finish the workday feeling less stiff.
blocks.detail: One practical change to how you sit, move or organize a task can make long desk days far more comfortable.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows how to fit your desk and chair to you.

blocks.text: Mobility means moving your joints through a range you can comfortably control. At a desk, that could mean turning toward a coworker or moving your ankles while seated. It doesn’t mean a dramatic stretch or proving how flexible you are.

The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS) says no single working position suits anyone for long, so changing position matters. Ergonomics means fitting the work and equipment to the person doing it. Canada’s movement guidelines also suggest sitting no more than 8 hours a day in total and breaking up long stretches of sitting as often as you can.

This lesson offers general examples, not treatment for an injury. If movement brings pain, numbness or dizziness, stop. Ask a health professional about new, ongoing or worsening symptoms before choosing moves that might make them worse.
Start with the task you do most. After you adjust something, try that task and notice whether you can do it without reaching or leaning awkwardly.
Check the chair and desk

Use the chair controls to support your lower back and leave room for your legs. Your feet should rest on the floor or a footrest. If raising the chair helps you reach a high desk but leaves your feet dangling, review the whole setup.
At a shared desk, take a minute to learn the controls before you start. A setting that suited the last person may not suit you, and a label like “ergonomic” doesn’t remove the need to adjust it.
Bring the task closer

Keep things you use often within easy reach, with room to shift position. Clear bags from under the desk. If the layout keeps forcing a long reach, ask for help changing it instead of trying to stretch away the problem.

Put your main screen where you can read it without constantly turning or craning your neck. About an arm’s length away is a starting point, adjusted for your eyesight and task. Larger text can help you read without leaning in. People who wear reading lenses or bifocals may need a lower screen.

A laptop joins the screen and keyboard together. If it’s your everyday workstation, ask your workplace about a separate keyboard, mouse or screen, instead of assuming one laptop angle can work for both.

items.title: “A standing desk means you should stand all day.”
items.text: Standing for long periods can cause discomfort too. A sit/stand desk gives you another position to choose, and it still needs to fit you both sitting and standing.

blocks.text: Write down one problem before you shop for equipment. A workplace ergonomics contact or supervisor may help you test a change.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The payroll deadline

blocks.text: The payroll deadline
paragraphs: Nadia worked as a payroll clerk in Calgary and wanted to finish Friday’s pay run without taking a pile of corrections home. She had a careful checklist and a calendar full of short calls. By Wednesday afternoon, her shoulders ached from hours of checking entries on two screens.

At first she blamed the busiest week of the month. Then a teammate borrowed her desk and asked why the payroll screen was way off to the left. Months ago, Nadia had moved it to make room for a paper tray, and she had stopped noticing how often she turned toward it.

She worried that fixing the desk would waste time before the deadline. Buying a standing desk also felt easier than explaining the problem to her supervisor. Instead, she asked for ten minutes to look at her setup and how the team handled breaks between checks.

They moved the main screen in front of her and found a nearby shelf for the tray. Her supervisor helped plan a few tasks away from the desk during the day. Nadia also stuck a note beside her checklist to pause after each finished batch, instead of waiting until every record was done.

On Thursday, she discovered that the tray held forms another team had stopped using months ago. The tray could go altogether, giving her even more space. Nobody needed an expensive desk to solve that part.

Friday still brought a late correction, and Nadia wasn’t comfortable every minute. But she finished the pay run at work and wrote down the changes worth keeping. Her checklist now had a spot for a pause, so the calendar no longer made every decision about her day.

blocks.text: How often you can move depends partly on how work is organized. If calls, deadlines or coverage get in the way, talk about the task schedule with the person who can help change it.
Name one problem clearly, and the fix is often simpler than you think.
blocks.detail: A clear description of one workspace problem helps you ask for practical support, and testing the change shows you what to keep.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a two-minute reset for your workday.

blocks.text: Choose a natural pause, such as finishing a document, and check that you have clear space. This two-minute reset is a learning example, not a rehab program or a required workplace break. Use only comfortable moves and breathe normally.
Example: a two-minute workday reset

items.title: First 30 seconds: release the keyboard and mouse, rest your hands, and let your shoulders settle.
Next 30 seconds: make a few small, slow shoulder rolls, then rest for the remaining time.
Next 30 seconds: while seated with support, gently lift and lower your heels a few times, then rest.
Final 30 seconds: change to another comfortable position, or walk slowly in a clear area if suitable.

blocks.text: Four 30-second blocks add up to two minutes. You can swap any block for quiet rest or stop early. There’s no target number of moves, and no need to fill every second.
CCOHS recommends 5 to 10 minutes away from your workstation for every hour you spend there, ideally walking or changing position. This short reset is an extra option. It doesn’t replace that advice.

For a seated option, make the last block a small, supported change of position. If standing suits you, hold a steady surface for balance as needed, never a rolling chair. Don’t bounce or force a stretch, and stop any move that causes pain or severe discomfort.

items.title: “A stretch only counts if you push farther each day.”
items.text: Comfortable movement doesn’t need a daily range goal. You can repeat the same gentle option, or skip it when it doesn’t suit you.

blocks.text: A movement plan needs a safe place. In icy weather, choose a clear indoor route instead of relying on an outdoor walk, and watch for wet floors near entrances.
Insider tip: Write your cue beside a task you already finish, like saving a report. If you keep missing it, change the cue or talk about a better work pause, instead of adding a louder reminder.

When you’re ready to adjust the plan, change one thing, such as the cue, before changing the moves. Keep the version that fits your day, and repeat it with no deadline to progress. Ongoing discomfort needs advice about the task and your symptoms, not a harder reset.
Quick Check

items.title: Does mobility require reaching your farthest possible stretch?
items.text: Use movement you can comfortably control.

items.title: What should you review if chair height leaves your feet hanging?
items.detail: Review the chair, desk and foot support together.

items.title: Does the two-minute example replace CCOHS workstation-break guidance?
items.text: It is a separate, optional short reset.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Sam reads tiny spreadsheet text by leaning toward the screen. What is a useful first step? A. Try larger text and review the screen position. · B. Hold the same lean all day. · C. Add stronger neck stretches.
items.text: Readable text and a suitable screen position address the task that causes the lean.

items.title: Jules feels tired feet after standing at a new desk all morning. What fits this lesson? A. Stand longer to meet a daily target. · B. Review the setup and change to another suitable position. · C. Remove all seated work.
items.text: The desk offers position choices. It needs to suit Jules when seated and standing.

items.title: A reset movement causes pain. What should Lee do? A. Finish the timed block. · B. Move faster. · C. Stop the movement and seek advice about ongoing symptoms.
items.text: The timer does not override pain. Symptoms that continue need suitable professional advice.

items.title: Write one task cue and one practical change you could use in your own workday.
items.text: After saving a report, I will check whether the tray beside my keyboard can move to a shelf. I will ask my supervisor before moving shared supplies.

blocks.text: Give yourself a choice of comfortable positions, check equipment fit, and plan time away from the workstation. A short reset can support that plan.
Write a small plan using the questions below. If you’re unsure whether a move suits you, make getting advice your first step.
Write your plan in your own words below. Keep it about work habits. It doesn’t need private health details.

items.title: Mobility
items.text: Movement through a joint range you can control comfortably.

items.title: Ergonomics
items.text: Fitting work and equipment to the person doing a task.

items.title: Workstation
items.text: The equipment and space used to do your work.

items.title: Position change
items.text: Moving from one supported working position to another.

items.title: Cue
items.text: A planned reminder linked to an event or task.

items.title: Reset
items.text: A short pause with optional comfortable movement.
